title: The Man Who Held Eighty-Two Numbers
author: Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool
wiifm: Every trade is full of people who have done the same job for twenty years and are no better than they were in year three, and a few who keep getting better. This is the story of Anders Ericsson, a Swedish psychologist who spent forty years asking what separates them, beginning with an undergraduate repeating numbers in a Pittsburgh lab. You will come away knowing what real practice contains, why a plateau is a problem of method rather than effort, and how far later research has cut his boldest claims down to size.

b: Karl Anders Ericsson was born in Stockholm in 1947, and for the first part of his career he was interested in something that sounded faintly unscientific: what actually goes on inside a person's head while they think. He took his doctorate at Stockholm University in 1976, and the following year he crossed the Atlantic to Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh to work with Herbert Simon, a restless polymath who would win the Nobel prize in economics in 1978 for his work on how real people make decisions.

Simon's group was obsessed with experts. A few years earlier, Simon and his colleague William Chase had shown that chess masters could glance at a position from a real game for a few seconds and rebuild it almost perfectly on an empty board. Ericsson's own speciality was asking people to think aloud while they solved problems, and treating their words as data. It was patient, unglamorous work, and it gave him the habit that would define his life. When someone does something extraordinary, do not admire it. Ask what they are doing, and then test it.

The question in the air was about limits. In 1956 the American psychologist George Miller had published a famous paper called The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two. Short-term memory, it said, holds about seven items. Textbooks treated that figure as wiring, about as changeable as your height.

Ericsson and Chase decided to find out what would happen if somebody simply trained, several times a week, for as long as it took. They needed a volunteer with patience and nothing to prove. They found an undergraduate called Steve Faloon.
ch.cap: Young Ericsson arrives at Simon's chess-obsessed Pittsburgh lab

ch.h: The runner who heard race times
b: The task was dull to the point of absurdity. A researcher read out random digits at one per second, and Faloon tried to repeat them back. In his first sessions he managed about seven, sometimes eight, exactly as the textbook predicted. After a handful of sessions he told the researchers he thought his limit was somewhere around eight or nine. Any sensible person would have agreed with him.

The protocol, though, was cleverer than the task. If Faloon got a string right, the next one was a digit longer. If he got it wrong, the next one was two digits shorter. He was never allowed to settle at a comfortable level. He lived permanently on the edge of failure, which is an unpleasant place to work and an extremely efficient one. After every attempt he talked through what he had been doing, so the researchers could see where it had gone wrong.

His first breakthrough came from his other life. Faloon was a keen distance runner, and he began to hear groups of digits as race times. Three, four, nine, two stopped being four separate numbers and became three minutes forty-nine point two seconds, a very fast mile. He was not stretching his short-term memory at all. He was building a way to hang new information on things he already knew deeply, so it could be stored in long-term memory fast enough to keep up.

Two years and more than two hundred sessions later, Faloon could hear a string of eighty-two random digits read out at one a second and give every one of them back in order. Ericsson, Chase and Faloon published the result in the journal Science in 1980. A supposed law of the mind had turned out to be a description of untrained people.
ch.cap: Faloon hears random digits as mile times: 3:49.2

b: The most useful part of the Faloon story is not the ending. It is the walls he hit on the way. At around twenty-two digits he stuck fast, and for weeks no amount of effort shifted him. Trying harder did nothing at all.

What moved him was a change of method. He began mixing groups of three digits with groups of four, and he built a hierarchy on top of them, groups of groups, so he could find his way around a long string rather than reciting it from the start. He climbed again, into the thirties. Then he stalled again, and changed method again. That cycle, repeated for two years, is the whole of Ericsson's later book in miniature.

Ericsson took a lesson from it that he spent the rest of his life repeating. When progress stops, the problem is almost never the amount of effort. It is the way you are holding the task in your head. A plateau is not a ceiling. It is a sign that your current method has given you everything it has, and that you need to try differently rather than harder.

There was a revealing footnote. When the researchers tested Faloon on letters instead of digits, his span fell straight back to about six. Two years of training had not given him a better memory. It had given him a better system for one kind of material. Skill, Ericsson concluded, is specific. You get good at exactly what you practise, in exactly the way you practise it, and almost nothing else.
ch.cap: Stuck at twenty-two, Faloon climbs by grouping digits differently

b: Over the following decades Ericsson grew irritated with the way English uses a single word for very different activities. In Peak, written with the science journalist Robert Pool and published in 2016, he separates them carefully, and the distinction is where most self-improvement quietly fails.

The first is naive practice: doing the thing again and again and hoping. It is the golfer who has played every Sunday for twenty years and is no better than in year three, or the manager who has had a thousand difficult conversations and is still bad at them. Repetition without a way of improving does not produce improvement. It produces automation, and once a skill runs on autopilot it stops developing and slowly starts to decay.

The second is purposeful practice, which is what Faloon was doing. It has four features, and all four matter. It has a specific, well-defined goal, not get better at sales but make the first ninety seconds of this call end with the customer asking a question. It demands full attention. It gives immediate feedback, so you know within seconds whether the attempt worked. And it happens just outside your comfort zone, where you fail a meaningful share of the time.

The third, deliberate practice, is purposeful practice plus two things most fields lack: an established body of knowledge about what excellence looks like, with objective ways to measure it, and a teacher who can design the training. Violin has that. Chess has it. Management, sales and running a small business mostly do not. In those fields you have to build both missing pieces yourself: a clear picture of what good looks like, and honest, fast feedback. That building job is the real work.
ch.cap: A salesman replays his call; outside, a golfer just repeats

b: The study that made Ericsson famous was carried out in Berlin, with his colleagues Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development. They went to the music academy in West Berlin and asked the violin professors to sort their students into three groups: the best, who were heading for international solo careers, the good, and a third group training to become music teachers rather than performers.

Then they reconstructed, through interviews and diaries, how much time each student had spent practising alone since childhood. The pattern looked startlingly clean. By the age of twenty, the best group had averaged around ten thousand hours of solitary practice. The good group had averaged nearer eight thousand, and the future teachers fewer than five thousand.

There were quieter findings too, and they are the more human ones. Every group agreed that practising alone was the most important thing they did to improve, and also one of the least enjoyable. The best players did not practise in long, miserable marathons. They worked in focused sessions, often in the morning, and they slept more than the others, including afternoon naps. Concentration this intense, Ericsson argued, can only be sustained for a few hours a day.

The paper appeared in Psychological Review in 1993. Its message was radical. The differences we put down to talent, it suggested, might largely be the accumulated result of years of a particular kind of effort. Ericsson moved to Florida State University in 1992, and spent the next quarter of a century defending that idea.
ch.cap: Berlin violinists practise alone; the best also nap

b: Why does practice have to hurt? Ericsson's answer is physiological, and it is the most satisfying mechanism in the book. The body and brain are built to stay as they are. Push a system only to the level it already handles, and nothing changes, because nothing needs to. Push it meaningfully past that level and you create a problem it can only solve by rebuilding itself.

His favourite evidence came from London taxi drivers. To drive a black cab you must pass the Knowledge, an examination on roughly twenty-five thousand streets and the quickest route between any two points, which usually takes three or four years of learning on a moped. The neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned drivers' brains and, in 2000, reported that they had a larger rear part of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, than other people. The front part was slightly smaller. The adaptation was a trade, not a free gift.

A later study by Maguire and Katherine Woollett, published in 2011, followed trainees over time. Those who qualified showed growth in that region. Those who failed or gave up showed no such change. The brain had not grown because these were special people. It grew because the demand was relentless and it had no other way to meet it.

There is a second half to this, which people skip. Push too far past your limit and you do not adapt either. You break, or you quit. The useful zone is narrow, just beyond what you can reliably do. Faloon's rule of one digit longer after success and two shorter after failure found that zone automatically. Any training you design for yourself needs something that does the same job, or you will drift back to comfortable difficulty without noticing.
ch.cap: A Knowledge boy memorises London as his hippocampus grows

b: Ask Ericsson what experts have that the rest of us lack, and he would not say hours or talent. He would say mental representations: patterns stored in long-term memory that let a person see a situation as a meaningful whole rather than a pile of parts.

Chess shows it best. Give a master a few seconds with a position from a real game and he can rebuild it almost perfectly. Give him the same number of pieces scattered at random and his advantage nearly vanishes. His memory is not better than yours. His library of meaningful patterns is enormous, and a random board contains none of them. He does not see thirty-two pieces. He sees a handful of familiar structures, the way you see a word rather than a string of letters.

This changes what practice is for. It is not mainly about muscle memory or piling up facts. It is about building representations that are richer and more finely tuned than the ones you have now. The experienced surgeon sees the tissue plane the trainee cannot. The experienced nurse walks onto a ward and senses that one patient is quietly deteriorating before the numbers say so. The good negotiator hears three meanings in a sentence you heard as one.

Representations are both the engine and the product of practice. Better ones let you spot your own mistakes more precisely, which makes your practice better, which builds better representations. That loop explains a common and discouraging experience: progress feels slow for a year and then suddenly fast. You were building the equipment to see with. Now you can use it.
ch.cap: The master sees shapes; the random board means nothing

b: In 2008 Malcolm Gladwell published Outliers. He read the Berlin violin paper, took the top group's average, and turned it into the ten-thousand-hour rule: practise anything for ten thousand hours and you will become world class. It became one of the most repeated ideas of the decade, and Ericsson spent much of the rest of his life objecting to it.

His objections were simple. Ten thousand was an average, not a threshold. Some of the best violinists had done considerably fewer hours, and some of the merely good had done more. The number had no magic in it. It was just what elite twenty-year-old violinists in Berlin happened to have accumulated. And Gladwell's version dropped the one thing that mattered most, which was the kind of practice. The popular rule tells people the answer is endurance. Ericsson's research said the answer was method.

Peak was partly written to set that straight. It also takes aim at talent as an explanation. Mozart's perfect pitch is often held up as proof of an inborn gift. Ericsson points out that Mozart was trained intensively from a very young age by a father who was a professional musician and teacher, and he cites a Japanese study, published in 2014 by Ayako Sakakibara, in which young children aged two to six were trained to perfect pitch with a structured method.

That does not prove nothing is innate. What it shows is how quickly we file a skill under talent simply because we never watched the training. And the belief matters. If ability is given, a plateau means you have found your ceiling and should stop. If ability is built, a plateau means your method has run out and you should change it. Only the second belief keeps you in the game long enough for training to work.
ch.cap: A bestseller turns an average into the 10,000-hour rule

b: Now the honest part, because Ericsson's central claim has taken real damage, and you should know where it stands before you build anything on it.

In 2014 the psychologists Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald published a meta-analysis in Psychological Science, pooling eighty-eight studies and more than eleven thousand participants. Across the lot, deliberate practice explained about twelve per cent of the differences in performance. The share varied by field: around twenty-six per cent in games, twenty-one in music, eighteen in sport, four in education, and less than one per cent in the professions. Their verdict was that practice is important, but not as important as had been argued.

Then, in 2019, Macnamara and Megha Maitra repeated the violin study with violinists at the Cleveland Institute of Music. Some of it held up. Practising alone was still rated the most important activity, and the good players had done more of it than the least accomplished. But accumulated practice explained about twenty-six per cent of the differences in skill rather than roughly half, the best and the good did not differ significantly in hours, and the best players reported doing less weekly solo practice than the good ones.

Ericsson fought back. He argued that the critics had counted many kinds of practice that did not meet his strict definition, and that measuring hours of anything was never his claim. There is something in that. But it also makes his theory harder to test, and the broad picture the critics drew has largely stood.
ch.cap: A storm of studies: practice explains twelve per cent

b: Anders Ericsson died in June 2020, aged seventy-two, still arguing about practice. What he leaves behind is smaller than the myth that grew around him, and more useful.

Deliberate practice is necessary. Nobody becomes excellent without a great deal of focused, feedback-rich work, and almost everyone underestimates how much is needed and how little of their own activity qualifies. But it is not sufficient, and it does not explain who reaches the very top. Among people who all train seriously, aptitude, starting age, the quality of teaching and plain luck all play a part.

The practical reading is cheerful. The modest figures come from studies of people who were already practising hard. For most of the skills that matter in your working life, you are nowhere near that group, and that is exactly where the returns on structured practice are largest.

So take the method and leave the slogan. Choose one thing you do repeatedly and do badly. Set a single specific target for the next attempt. Get feedback fast, from a recording, a number or an honest colleague. Work just past what you can reliably manage. And when you stall, as Steve Faloon stalled at twenty-two digits, do not grit your teeth. Change the method.
ch.cap: Dawn in Tallahassee: the method outlives the man

take: A plateau is a method signal
When progress stops, more effort at the same approach rarely helps. Change how you are doing the thing, as Faloon did when he broke his twenty-two digit wall by changing his grouping system.
Doing something a thousand times makes it automatic, and automatic skills stop improving. Twenty years of experience can be one year repeated twenty times.
A specific goal, full attention, immediate feedback and a difficulty just past your reliable limit. Drop any one and you are back to naive repetition.
Build the coach your field lacks
Most business skills have no objective measure and no teacher. Pick one number that moves when you improve and one person who will tell you the uncomfortable truth each month.
Body and brain only rebuild when current capacity is not enough. Design practice that sits just beyond your limit and pulls you back there when you drift.
Expertise is a library of mental representations. Study real cases in your work until you start recognising situations as wholes.
Capture the call or meeting you do most often, set one target for next time, and review it within a day. Three examined attempts beat thirty unexamined ones.
Hold the claim at its true size
Practice explains a real but modest share of performance among serious practitioners. Use it as a method, not as a promise that hours guarantee mastery.
recall: What was the rule in Steve Faloon's digit training, and why did it matter?
A correct string meant the next was one digit longer, and a mistake meant the next was two shorter. That kept him permanently just past his reliable limit, the zone where adaptation happens.
Why did Faloon's progress stall, and what got him moving again?

Effort stopped helping because his method had run out, first at around twenty-two digits. He moved again by changing the system, mixing group sizes and building groups of groups, which is Ericsson's point that you should try differently rather than harder.
What does deliberate practice need that purposeful practice does not?
An established field with objective measures of excellence and a teacher who can design the training. Most business skills lack both, so you must build your own standard and your own feedback.
Why is a chess master's memory no better than a novice's on a random board?
His advantage is a library of meaningful patterns from real games, not raw memory. A random board contains none of those patterns, so he has nothing to compress it into.
What did the 2014 meta-analysis and the 2019 violin replication find?

The meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about twelve per cent of performance differences overall, much less in education and the professions. The replication found practice explained about a quarter of violin skill differences, with no significant gap in hours between the best and the good players.
note: Based on Peak, Ericsson, Chase and Faloon in Science, 1980, and Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer in Psychological Review, 1993. The taxi driver findings are Maguire and colleagues, 2000, and Woollett and Maguire, 2011. The main challenges are Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald, 2014, and Macnamara and Maitra, 2019, which Ericsson disputed on definitional grounds; the critics' broad conclusion is now widely accepted.
words: The tendency of a body or system to hold itself steady and resist change.
Ericsson argued that brain and body only rebuild when practice pushes them past what they already handle, overriding their homeostasis.
A device or system that makes something easier to remember by linking it to what you already know.
Steve Faloon's trick of hearing digits as running times was a mnemonic that let him hang random numbers on knowledge he already had.
A line that a curve approaches more and more closely without ever reaching it.
Faloon's progress at twenty-two digits looked like an asymptote, a natural ceiling, until a change of method sent him climbing again.
To treat an abstract idea or average as though it were a concrete, fixed thing.
Ericsson complained that the ten-thousand-hour rule reified an average from Berlin violinists into a universal threshold.
A study that pools the results of many earlier studies to estimate an overall effect.
Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald's 2014 meta-analysis of eighty-eight studies found deliberate practice explained about twelve per cent of performance differences.
stories: The man who held eighty-two numbers

In 1978 an undergraduate called Steve Faloon sat in a Carnegie Mellon lab repeating random digits read at one a second. He started at about seven, exactly what the textbooks said short-term memory could hold, and thought his limit was eight or nine. The rule was harsh: get one right and the next string was a digit longer, miss and it was two shorter. Faloon was a runner, and he began hearing digits as race times. Two years and over two hundred sessions later he could recall eighty-two. Then they tested him on letters, and he was back to about six. He had not built a better memory. He had built a better system.

To drive a black cab in London you must pass the Knowledge: roughly twenty-five thousand streets and the quickest route between any two, usually three or four years of learning on a moped. In 2000 the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned drivers' brains and found the rear of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger than in other people, while the front was slightly smaller. In 2011 she and Katherine Woollett followed trainees over time. The ones who qualified showed growth. The ones who failed or gave up did not. The brain had not grown because they were special. It grew because the demand left it no choice.

In the late 1980s Ericsson and his colleagues asked violin professors in West Berlin to sort their students into the best, the good, and future teachers. By twenty, the best had averaged around ten thousand hours of solitary practice, the good nearer eight thousand, the teachers under five. In 2008 Malcolm Gladwell turned that average into the ten-thousand-hour rule, and it became one of the most repeated ideas of the decade. Ericsson spent years objecting. Ten thousand was an average, not a threshold, and the rule left out the only thing that mattered, which was the kind of practice. Later studies cut even his own claims down to size.
biz: Most enquiry calls at HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan are naive practice: the same opening done a thousand times and never examined. Pick one target for the first ninety seconds, such as the customer understanding that you are a broker, not a lender, and what happens next, and ending with them asking a question. Record calls with proper disclosure, and each week review three against that single target with one honest colleague. Measure one number that moves with skill, like the share of first calls where the customer can state the next step. The aim is clarity under Consumer Duty, never more pressure.
When conversion stalls, change the method

If the enquiry-to-application rate has sat flat for six weeks, Faloon's lesson is that more effort at the same approach will not shift it. Do not simply ask for more leads or more calls. Change how the task is held: test a rewritten first WhatsApp message, a call within five minutes instead of an hour, or a clearer explanation of what documents a lender needs. Run one change at a time for two weeks and compare against the baseline. For ad and landing page changes, brief Grok with the hypothesis rather than raising budgets, so the plateau gets a new method rather than more spend.
connects: Kahneman argues expert intuition can only be trusted where the environment gives regular, fast feedback, which is exactly the condition Ericsson says real practice requires.
Pinker's case that inborn differences are real is the other side of the talent debate that Ericsson's critics reopened with their meta-analyses.
Greene stretches Ericsson's idea of mental representations across a whole career, calling the finished product intuition.
recap:
In nineteen seventy-seven a young Swedish psychologist called Anders Ericsson arrived in Pittsburgh to work with Herbert Simon, a future Nobel prize winner obsessed with experts. Ericsson had one habit that would shape his life. When someone does something extraordinary, do not admire it. Ask what they are doing, and test it.

The textbooks said short-term memory holds about seven items. So Ericsson and William Chase found an undergraduate, Steve Faloon, and read him random digits, one a second. At first he managed seven. The rule was cruel and clever. Get a string right and the next was one digit longer. Get it wrong and it was two shorter. Faloon lived on the edge of failure. He was a runner, and he began to hear digits as race times. Two years and more than two hundred sessions later, he could hold eighty-two. A law of the mind had turned out to describe untrained people.

The most useful moment came in the middle. At twenty-two digits Faloon stuck for weeks, and trying harder did nothing. What moved him was a new method, mixing groups of three and four. That is the first big idea. A plateau is not a ceiling. It is a sign to try differently, not harder.

The second idea is that practice comes in kinds. Naive practice is repetition and hope, and it produces autopilot. Purposeful practice has a specific goal, full attention, fast feedback, and difficulty just past your limit. Deliberate practice adds a teacher and a clear picture of excellence, which most businesses lack, so you have to build them yourself.

The third idea is that discomfort is the mechanism. London cab drivers who passed the Knowledge grew the part of the brain that handles spatial memory. Those who quit did not. The fourth is that experts see patterns, not parts, the way a chess master sees shapes rather than pieces.

In Berlin, Ericsson found the best young violinists had practised alone for around ten thousand hours by twenty. Malcolm Gladwell turned that average into a rule, and Ericsson spent years protesting that the kind of practice mattered more than the count. Then the critics came. A large review in twenty fourteen found practice explained about twelve per cent of performance differences. Ericsson disputed it, but the broad picture stood.

He died in twenty twenty, still arguing. What survives is smaller than the myth and more useful. Practice is necessary, not sufficient, and most of us are nowhere near the point where it stops paying.

When you stall, do not grit your teeth. Change the method.
